_**Agent (auto-smart)**_

That claim is clearer: different perspectives matter, De Bono is the mental model, and you’re skeptical that five subagents are worth the cost.

**Quick compare (so we’re aligned before drafting):**

| Council lens | Closest hat | Fit |
|---|---|---|
| Contrarian | Black | Strong — risk, what’s wrong |
| Expansionist | Yellow | Strong — upside if it works |
| First Principles | White + a bit of Green | Partial — facts/assumptions more than wild ideas |
| Outsider | (no hat) | Fresh eyes / curse-of-knowledge; De Bono doesn’t isolate this |
| Executor | (no hat) | “Monday morning” action; hats stay in thinking, not shipping |
| Chairman | Blue | Strong — process + synthesis |
| (missing) | Red | Feelings/intuition aren’t a dedicated advisor |
| (missing) | Green as pure creativity | First Principles isn’t the same as “invent options” |

**On subagents vs one agent:** you’re right that five subagents cost more — more context windows, more tokens, parallel Task runs. The skill wants separate agents so each answer is written *before* it sees the others; peer review only works if they didn’t already negotiate in one head. One agent wearing five hats is cheaper and often good enough for a personal archive. Full council earns the cost when being wrong is expensive (pricing, hire, retire a post that still gets traffic). For “pressure-test my blog,” one sequential pass can be enough; you already proved the *method* works either way.

**Interview Q3:** After reading, what should someone feel or do — try a cheaper one-agent “hats” pass on their own work, understand when full council is worth the bill, or something else?
